titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The battle against Yúsuf and the great spoil (tirada 95, lines 1711–1798)
part: Tirada 95 · The battle against Yúsuf and the great spoil (lines 1711–1798)

sentences.t:
Salidos son todos armados por las torres de [Quarto],
mio Çid a los sos vassallos tan bien los acordando.
Dexan a las puertas omnes de grant recabdo.
sentences.l:
They-have gone-out all armed by the towers of [Quarto],
my Çid to the his vassals so well them admonishing.
They-leave at the gates men of great trust.
sentences.i: They have all ridden out in arms by the towers of Quarto, my Çid giving his vassals good counsel all the while. At the gates they leave men they can trust.
sentences.n: Tirada 95 (assonance á-o) — the Christians go out to battle; Yúsuf routed; an extraordinary booty; the Çid greets his wife and daughters and dowers Ximena's ladies; the sharing of the spoil (Pidal: Los cristianos salen a batalla.—Derrota de Yúcef. Botín extraordinario.—El Cid saluda a su mujer y sus hijas. Dota a las dueñas de Jimena. Reparto del botín). The line-ends run armados, acordando, recabdo, cavallo, adobado, salto: stressed á, then o, kept to the end of the tirada. Salidos son, 'they have gone out', ser + participle with a verb of motion. [Quarto], the whole word Pidal's restoration (in italics): Pidal's note: Quarto is a place at the fourth milestone (cuarto miliario) of the road from Valencia toward Castile, and las torres de Cuarto (Valencian torres de Cuart) are the towers on either side of the gate in Valencia's wall that opens on the road to Cuart; the towers standing now are of the fifteenth century, on a widening of the older wall, which also had its gate and towers of Cuarto. acordando, 'instructing, admonishing' (acordar, to bring to one mind); Pidal's note: 'mio Cid previniendo o aleccionando muy bien a sus vasallos', forewarning or schooling his men well: the gerund runs on loosely from the main verb; los repeats a los sos vassallos, the a marking a personal object. omnes = hombres; de grant recabdo, 'of great care', men to be relied on (recabdo, 'care, prudence', later in this tirada 'reckoning').

sentences.t:
Dió salto mio Çid en Bavieca el so cavallo;
de todas guarnizones muy bien es adobado.
sentences.l:
Gave leap my Çid on Bavieca the his horse;
of all trappings very well he-is equipped.
sentences.i: My Çid sprang out on Babieca, his horse, splendidly fitted with all his gear.
sentences.n: Dió salto, 'he leapt out', 'he sallied' (dar salto, as in tirada 92). Bavieca, the Çid's horse (Babieca). el so cavallo, article + possessive, 'his horse'; so = su. guarnizones, 'trappings, armour, harness'. adobado, 'equipped, armed' (adobar).

sentences.i: They carry the banner out and sally from Valencia, four thousand less thirty riding with my Çid; gladly they go to strike the fifty thousand.
sentences.n: seña, 'banner, standard'. Epic tense-mixing: sacan (present), dieron (preterite), van (present). van a cabo, most likely 'go along, go to the end' with him, 'ride out in his company'; the shade of a cabo here is not certain. a los çinquaenta mill vanlos ferir, 'the fifty thousand they go to strike them', the personal object with a, then picked up again by los; ferir = herir (f- for h-). de grado, 'willingly, gladly'. The full stop at the end of v. 1717 and the small a of v. 1718 are Pidal's print.

sentences.t:
Álvar Alvar[oz] e Minaya entráronles del otro cabo.
Plogo al Criador e ovieron de arrancarlos.
sentences.l:
Álvar Alvar[oz] and Minaya entered-on-them from-the other side.
It-pleased to-the Creator and they-had to rout-them.
sentences.i: Álvar Álvarez and Minaya fell on them from the other side. It pleased the Creator, and they put them to rout.
sentences.n: Pidal prints this verse with two numbers, 1719-20; the line keeps both places in the traditional count. Álvar Alvar[oz] = Álvar Álvarez, one of the Çid's knights (Álbar Albar[oz] at v. 739, Álvar Álvarez in the translation there too), the -oz ending Pidal's (in italics). This is Minaya's flanking attack, that he asked for in tirada 93. entráronles, 'they came in on them', les the Moors. del otro cabo, 'from the other side' (cabo, 'end, side'). Plogo, preterite of plazer, 'it pleased'. ovieron de arrancarlos, aver de + infinitive, 'they came to rout them'; arrancar, the poem's word for routing an army in the field.

sentences.i: My Çid spent his lance and set his hand to his sword; so many Moors he kills that they were never counted, the blood running down past his elbow.
sentences.n: enpleó la lança, 'he used up the lance': Pidal's note, the Çid used the lance and, once he had broken it, put his hand to the sword (introduction, p. 101). al espada = a el espada, el the old article before a vowel (espada is feminine). atantos, 'so many'. cobdo = codo, 'elbow'; ayuso, 'down', 'downward'; destellando, 'dripping' (destellar, Latin destillare, from stilla, 'a drop'): the gerund hangs loose, the picture of the sword-arm.

sentences.i: He had dealt King Yúsuf three blows, but Yúsuf slipped out from under his sword, for his horse ran hard for him, and got away from him into Gujera, a stately castle.
sentences.n: tres colpes le ovo dados, 'he had dealt him three blows', the participle dados agreeing with its object colpes (colpe = golpe). saliósle, 'he got away from him', the se of the verb and le, 'from him' (the Çid). del sol espada, most likely 'from under the sword', so = 'under' (Latin sub) with the article reduced to l before espada; the run of letters is hard to divide, and the exact construction is uncertain, though the sense is not. ca muchol andido el cavallo, 'for his horse went hard for him': muchol = mucho le; andido, the old strong preterite of andar (= anduvo). metiósle, 'he got himself in, away from him'. Gujera, Cullera (Pidal's note: 'Cullera', v. 1160), the castle on the coast south of Valencia. palaçiano, 'palatial, stately'.

sentences.t:
mio Çid el de Bivar fasta allí llegó en alca[nço]
con otros quel consiguen de s[o]s buenos vassallos.
sentences.l:
my Çid he of Bivar up-to there arrived in pur[suit]
with others who-him follow of h[i]s good vassals.
sentences.i: My Çid of Bivar came there in pursuit, with others of his good vassals who kept up with him.
sentences.n: alca[nço], 'pursuit' (modern alcance; compare alcaz in tirada 93), the nço Pidal's (in italics). quel = que le; consiguen, 'follow, catch up with'. s[o]s = sus, the o Pidal's (in italics).

sentences.t:
Desd' allí se tornó el que en buen ora nasco,
mucho era alegre de lo que an caçado;
allí preçió a Bavieca de la cabeça fasta a cabo.
Toda esta ganançia en su mano a rastado.
sentences.l:
From there himself turned he who in good hour was-born,
much he-was glad of that which they-have taken;
there he-prized Bavieca from the head up-to end.
All this gain in his hand has remained.
sentences.i: From there he turned back, he who was born in a good hour, very glad of what they had taken; there he praised Babieca from head to tail. All this winning has stayed in his hand.
sentences.n: el que en buen ora nasco, the formula 'he who was born in a good hour'; nasco, old strong preterite of naçer (= nació). an caçado, 'they have taken': Pidal's note, caçar is 'coger', 'to take, catch' in general (Latin captare, captiare), not yet narrowed to what is taken by hunting. preçió, 'he prized, praised' (preçiar), Babieca de la cabeça fasta a cabo, 'from head to end'. a rastado, 'has remained', rastar as in the Çid's speech of tirada 93; Pidal's note: 'quedar' (ha quedado por suya), it has remained his.

sentences.t:
Los çinquaenta mill por cuenta fuero' notados:
non escaparon mas de çiento e quatro.
sentences.l:
The fifty thousand by count were noted:
not escaped more than hundred and four.
sentences.i: The fifty thousand were taken down by count: no more than a hundred and four escaped.
sentences.n: fuero' = fueron, the apostrophe Pidal's: the final n lost before the n of notados. por cuenta, 'by count, by tally'. mas de, 'more than'.

sentences.i: My Çid's companies have plundered the field: in gold and silver together they found three thousand marks, and of the rest of the spoil there was no reckoning.
sentences.n: mesnadas, 'household companies'. robado an, 'they have plundered', the auxiliary after the participle. entre oro e plata, 'gold and silver together'. marcos, the mark, a weight of silver or gold (about half a pound). [de], Pidal's (in italics). non avía recabdo, 'there was no account', aver impersonal, 'there was'.

sentences.t:
Alegre era mio Çid e todos sos vassallos,
que Dios les ovo merçed que vençieron el campo:
sentences.l:
Glad was my Çid and all his vassals,
that God to-them had mercy that they-conquered the field:
sentences.i: Glad was my Çid and all his vassals that God had shown them the grace to win the field.
sentences.n: ovo merçed, 'had mercy, showed favour', aver as full verb. vençieron el campo, 'they won the field'.

sentences.i: When they had routed the King of Morocco in this way, he left Álvar Fáñez to take a full reckoning, and with a hundred knights he has entered Valencia.
sentences.n: al rey de Marruecos … lo an arrancado, the personal object with a, picked up again by lo. dexó Álbar Fáñez, 'he left Álvar Fáñez' (Minaya) behind on the field; por saber todo recabdo, 'to learn the whole account', to tally the spoil (vv. 1772–1773). es entrado, ser + participle with a verb of motion.

sentences.t:
fronzida trahe la cara, que era desarmado,
assí entró sobre Bavieca, el espada en la mano.
sentences.l:
wrinkled he-brings the face, for he-was unarmed,
thus he-entered upon Bavieca, the sword in the hand.
sentences.i: He comes with his coif gathered about his face, for he had taken off his helmet and mail hood, and so he rode in on Babieca, sword in hand.
sentences.n: fronzida, 'wrinkled, gathered' (= fruncida; compare French froncer). Pidal's note: fronzida la cara, as at v. 2436, is to be understood of the coif gathered about the face (la cofia fronzida, v. 789), and era desarmado means that he had taken off his defensive arms, the helmet and the mail hood (almófar), as was done as soon as the fighting stopped, to cool the head; he compares vv. 789–90 and 2436–37. trahe = trae, 'he brings, wears'. el espada, el the old article before a vowel.

sentences.t:
Reçibienlo las dueñas que lo están esperando;
mio Çid fincó antellas, tovo la rienda al cavallo:
sentences.l:
Were-receiving-him the ladies who him are awaiting;
my Çid stopped before-them, held the rein to-the horse:
sentences.i: The ladies who are waiting for him come out to receive him; my Çid halted before them and reined in his horse:
sentences.n: Reçibienlo, imperfect in -ie (= recibíanlo). dueñas, 'ladies', Ximena, her daughters and their women. fincó, 'stopped, stayed' (fincar, f- for h-). antellas = ante ellas. tovo, preterite of tener, 'held'.

sentences.t:
“A vos me omillo, dueñas, grant prez vos he gañado:
vos teniendo Valençia, e yo vençí el campo;
esto Dios se lo quiso con todos los sos santos,
quando en vuestra venida tal ganançia nos han dad[o].
sentences.l:
“To you myself I-humble, ladies, great worth for-you I-have won:
you holding Valencia, and I conquered the field;
this God himself it willed with all the his saints,
when in your coming such gain to-us they-have give[n].
sentences.i: “I bow to you, ladies; I have won you great honour: while you held Valencia, I won the field. God willed it so, with all his saints, since at your coming they have given us such a gain.
sentences.n: me omillo, 'I bow down, humble myself' (omillarse); Pidal's note: a vos me omillo, the usual formula of greeting (v. 1396). prez, 'worth, honour'. gañado = ganado, 'won' (the first letter is broken in the print; g is the reading). vos teniendo Valençia, an absolute gerund, 'you holding Valencia': the ladies kept the city while he fought. Dios se lo quiso, 'God himself willed it'. han dad[o], plural, God and his saints together; the o Pidal's (in italics).

sentences.t:
Ve[e]des el espada sangrienta e sudiento el cavallo:
con tal cum esto se vençen moros del campo.
sentences.l:
You-s[e]e the sword bloody and sweating the horse:
with such as this themselves are-conquered Moors of-the field.
sentences.i: You see the sword all bloody and the horse in a sweat: this is how Moors are beaten in the field.
sentences.n: Ve[e]des = veis, 'you see', from the old two-syllable veer, the second e Pidal's (in italics). sudiento, 'sweating'. con tal cum esto, 'with such as this', cum = como; Pidal's note: 'de este modo', 'así', 'in this way'. se vençen, the passive se, 'are conquered'.

sentences.t:
Rogad al Criador que vos viba algunt año,
entraredes en prez, e besarán vuestras manos.”
Esto dixo mio Çid, diçiendo del cavallo.
sentences.l:
Pray to-the Creator that for-you I-may-live some year,
you-will-enter into worth, and they-will-kiss your hands.”
This said my Çid, descending from-the horse.
sentences.i: Pray to the Creator that I may live some years for you: you will come into honour, and men will kiss your hands.” So my Çid spoke, getting down from his horse.
sentences.n: que vos viba algunt año, 'that I may live for you some year', viba = viva, subjunctive, the subject I understood. entraredes en prez, 'you will enter into honour'. besarán vuestras manos, the hand-kiss of homage; Pidal's note: 'tendréis vasallos', 'you will have vassals' (compare v. 3450, and vos besa las manos commo vassallo a señor, v. 2948): already ladies of Valencia, they will have more vassals still. diçiendo, 'descending', from deçir (Latin descendere), not dezir 'to say'; Pidal's note: 'apeándose', 'dismounting' (v. 1394).

sentences.t:
Quandol vieron de pie que era descavalgado,
las dueñas e las fijas, e la mugier que vale algo
delant el Campeador los inojos fincaron:
“Somos en vuestra merced, e bivades muchos años!”
sentences.l:
When-him they-saw on foot that he-was dismounted,
the ladies and the daughters, and the wife who is-worth something
before the Campeador the knees they-planted:
“We-are in your grace, and may-you-live many years!”
sentences.i: When they saw him on foot, dismounted, the ladies and the daughters and his wife, a woman of worth, knelt before the Campeador: “We are at your mercy, and may you live many years!”
sentences.n: Quandol = quando le, 'when him'. de pie, 'on foot'. la mugier que vale algo, 'the wife who is worth something', a lady of worth; algo, 'something, worth, property'. los inojos fincaron, 'they planted their knees', 'knelt' (inojos = hinojos). merced is spelled here with plain c (merçed at v. 1740). bivades, subjunctive of bivir, 'may you live'.

sentences.t:
En buelta con él entraron al palaçio,
e ivan posar con él en unos preçiosos escaños.
sentences.l:
In company with him they-entered to-the palace,
and they-were-going to-sit with him on some precious benches.
sentences.i: Together with him they went into the palace, and went to sit with him on fine benches.
sentences.n: En buelta con él, 'together with him' (buelta = vuelta, 'mingling'). ivan posar, ir + infinitive without a, 'they went to sit'. escaños, 'benches, settles', the seats of honour.

sentences.i: “Doña Ximena, my wife, had you not asked me this? These ladies you brought with you, who serve you so well, I mean to marry them to some of these vassals of mine;
sentences.n: Ya, 'oh', calling to her. d[o]ña, the o Pidal's (in italics). nom = non me, 'not me'. aviedes rogado, 'you had asked', imperfect of aver in -ie as the auxiliary; just what she had asked is not told. aduxiestes, preterite of aduzir, 'to bring'. quiérolas casar, 'I want to marry them', the pronoun glued to querer. con de aquestos mios vassallos, the partitive de, 'with some of these my vassals' (Pidal's note: 'con algunos de aquestos').

sentences.t:
a cada una dellas doles dozientos marcos,
que lo sepan en Castiella, a quién sirvieron tanto.
Lo de vuestras fijas venir se a más por espacio.”
sentences.l:
to each one of-them I-give-them two-hundred marks,
that it they-may-know in Castile, whom they-served so-much.
That of your daughters to-come itself will more at leisure.”
sentences.i: to each of them I give two hundred marks, so that in Castile they may know whom they served so well. Your daughters' turn will come later, at more leisure.”
sentences.n: doles, 'I give them', present for a firm promise. a quién sirvieron tanto, 'whom they served so well': the dowry shows Castile what a lord they had. venir se a = se vendrá, 'will come', the split future: the infinitive, se, then a (= ha). Lo de vuestras fijas, 'the matter of your daughters', their marriages. por espacio (so printed, with plain c), 'slowly, at leisure'.

sentences.t:
Levantáronse todas e besáronle las manos,
grant f[o] el alegría que f[o] por el palaçio.
Commo lo dixo el Çid, assí lo han acabado.
sentences.l:
They-rose all and kissed-him the hands,
great wa[s] the joy that wa[s] through the palace.
As it said the Çid, so it they-have accomplished.
sentences.i: They all rose and kissed his hands, and great was the joy throughout the palace. As the Çid had said it, so they have carried it out.
sentences.n: besáronle las manos, 'they kissed his hands', the dative le for the possessor; Pidal's note: they kiss the Çid's hand in thanks for the dowry he grants them (compare vv. 159, 692). f[o] = fue, the o Pidal's (in italics) both times. el alegría, el the old article before a vowel. acabado, 'carried through, accomplished' (Pidal's note: 'lo han llevado a cabo', 'lo han hecho').

sentences.t:
Minaya Álbar Fáñez fuera era en el campo,
con todas estas yentes escriviendo e contando;
entre tiendas e armas e vestidos preçiados
tanto fallan [ellos] desto que [mucho] es sobejano.
sentences.l:
Minaya Álbar Fáñez outside was in the field,
with all these people writing and counting;
between tents and arms and garments prized
so-much find [they] of-this that [much] it-is excessive.
sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez was out on the field with all these men, writing and counting; what with tents and arms and rich clothing, they find so much of it that it passes all measure.
sentences.n: yentes = gentes. escriviendo e contando, the tally Minaya was left to make (v. 1742); Pidal's note: Minaya at the head of the quiñoneros, the men who shared out the booty (introduction, p. 98). preçiados, 'prized, precious'. [ellos] and [mucho] are Pidal's (in italics). sobejano, 'excessive, overwhelming'.

sentences.i: I want to tell you what is greater still: they could not learn the count of all the horses running about in their harness with no one to take them; the Moors of the countryside got something there for themselves.
sentences.n: Quiérovos dezir, the singer addressing his hearers. granado, 'great, abundant'. arriados: Pidal's note gives 'andan arreados y no hay quien los tome', keeping the word; most likely 'in harness, in their trappings' (arreos), the horses of the beaten army running riderless with their gear still on; arrear also meant 'to drive (beasts)', and the exact shade is uncertain. non ha qui tomallos, 'there is no one to take them': ha impersonal, 'there is'; qui = quien; tomallos = tomarlos, the r assimilated to l. ganado se an y algo, 'they have won something there for themselves', the auxiliary after the participle; y = allí.

sentences.t:
maguer de todo esto, el Campeador contado
de los buenos e otorgados cayéronle mill cavallos;
quando a mio Çid cayeron tantos,
los otros bien pueden fincar pagados.
sentences.l:
although of all this, the Campeador renowned
of the good and approved fell-to-him thousand horses;
when to my Çid fell so-many,
the others well can remain paid.
sentences.i: Even so, to the renowned Campeador there fell a thousand horses of the good and proven sort; when so many fell to my Çid, the others may well be content.
sentences.n: maguer de todo esto, 'in spite of all this' (Pidal's note: maguer de, 'a pesar de'). contado, 'renowned', an epithet of the Campeador. otorgados, most likely 'approved, warranted' as sound (Pidal gives no note; the shade is not certain). cayéronle, 'fell to him' as his share. pagados, 'paid, satisfied'. Pidal numbers the last line 1782b, outside the traditional count.

sentences.t:
Tanta tienda preciada e tanto tendal obrado
que a ganado mio Çid con todos s[o]s vassallos!
sentences.l:
So-much tent prized and so-much tent-pole worked
that has won my Çid with all h[i]s vassals!
sentences.i: So many costly tents, so many worked tent-poles my Çid has won with all his vassals!
sentences.n: tienda, 'tent'; tendal, 'tent-pole'; obrado, 'worked, decorated': Pidal's note on tendal obrado (compare v. 2401), a pole with ornament, inlay and precious stones, or silver, as in other descriptions of rich tents, or gold, as at v. 1786. The singulars (tanta tienda, tanto tendal) stand for many. preciada is spelled here with plain c (preçiados at v. 1774). s[o]s = sus, the o Pidal's (in italics).

sentences.t:
La tienda del rey de Marruecos, que de las otras es cabo,
dos tendales la sufren, con oro son labrados;
sentences.l:
The tent of-the king of Marruecos, which of the others is head,
two tent-poles it hold-up, with gold they-are worked;
sentences.i: The King of Morocco's tent, the chief of them all, is borne up by two poles worked with gold;
sentences.n: que de las otras es cabo, 'which is the head of the others', cabo, 'head, chief'. la sufren, 'hold it up' (sufrir, Latin sufferre, 'to bear'). labrados, 'worked, wrought'. Pidal's note: a long tent on an elliptical base, its two centres marked by the two poles.

sentences.t:
mandó mio Çid [el Campeador contado],
que fita sovisse la tienda, e non la tolliesse dent cristiano:
sentences.l:
ordered my Çid [the Campeador renowned],
that fixed should-stay the tent, and not it should-take from-there Christian:
sentences.i: my Çid, the renowned Campeador, gave orders that the tent should be left standing, and that no one should take it away from there:
sentences.n: [el Campeador contado], the second half of the line wholly Pidal's restoration (in italics). fita, 'fixed, standing' (Latin fictus, from figere; = hincada). sovisse, imperfect subjunctive of seer (Latin sedere; old preterite sovo), 'should be, stay'; Pidal's note: fita sovisse, 'quedase plantada', 'should stay pitched', sovisse a dialect form of soviese, from seder (compare v. 1820). tolliesse, imperfect subjunctive of toller, 'to take away'. dent, 'from there' (Latin de inde). cristiano, 'a Christian', with non 'no one' (Pidal's note: 'nadie', as at v. 29).

sentences.t:
“Tal tienda commo esta, que de Marruecos [h]a passado,
enbiar la quiero a Alfonsso el Castellano,
que croviesse s[u]s nuevas de mio Çid que avíe algo.”
sentences.l:
“Such tent as this, which from Marruecos [h]as crossed,
to-send it I-want to Alfonsso the Castilian,
that he-might-believe [hi]s news of my Çid that he-had something.”
sentences.i: “A tent such as this, which has come over from Morocco, I mean to send to Alfonso the Castilian, so that he may believe the news of my Çid, that he has wealth.”
sentences.n: [h]a passado, 'has crossed', the h Pidal's (in italics): the tent has come over the sea from Africa. enbiar la quiero, 'I want to send it', the pronoun set between the infinitive and querer. Alfonsso el Castellano, King Alfonso VI, who exiled the Çid. Pidal's note on v. 1790: a later lapse of the poet (introduction, p. 84): the gift the Çid sends the king in the next tirada is two hundred horses (v. 1813), not the tent. croviesse, imperfect subjunctive of creer, from the old strong preterite crovo, 'that he might believe'. s[u]s nuevas de mio Çid, 'the news of my Çid', the Çid speaking of himself in the third person; the u Pidal's (in italics). que avíe algo, 'that he had something', 'that he had become rich'; avíe, imperfect in -ie of aver.

sentences.t: Con aquestas riquezas tantas a Valençia son entrados.
sentences.l: With these riches so-many to Valencia they-are entered.
sentences.i: With all these riches they have come into Valencia.
sentences.n: aquestas riquezas tantas, 'these so many riches', tantas set after the noun. son entrados, ser + participle with a verb of motion.

sentences.i: The bishop Don Jerome, an accomplished churchman, when he has had his fill of fighting with both his hands, keeps no count of the Moors he has killed; what fell to his share was beyond measure;
sentences.n: Jero[me], the ending Pidal's (in italics). caboso, 'accomplished, perfect'; coronado, 'crowned', that is tonsured, a cleric (as at vv. 1288, 1460). es farto, 'he is sated' (farto = harto, f- for h-), 'when he has fought his fill' (the speck between es and farto on the scan is a blemish, not a letter). amas las sus manos, 'both his hands', amas = ambas, with article + possessive. que ha matados, the participle agreeing with los moros. ca[d]ié, 'fell', imperfect in -ié of the old cader (= caer), the d Pidal's (in italics). sobejano, 'excessive', as at v. 1775.

sentences.t:
mio Çid don Rodrigo, el que en buen ora nasco,
de toda la su quinta el diezmo l'a mandado.
sentences.l:
my Çid don Rodrigo, he who in good hour was-born,
of all the his fifth the tithe to-him-has granted.
sentences.i: my Çid Don Rodrigo, he who was born in a good hour, has granted him the tithe of all his own fifth.
sentences.n: la su quinta, 'his fifth', the lord's fifth of all booty; of that the Çid gives the bishop a tenth, the church's tithe. l'a mandado = le ha mandado, 'has granted him' (Pidal's note: 'le ha otorgado el diezmo'; mandar 'to grant, assign', as at v. 1710), the le squeezed before a vowel. Here tirada 95 ends.
